newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Mindanao "promise" undimmed by wave of kidnapping.
newsitem.headline: Mindanao "promise" undimmed by wave of kidnapping.

text.p: Kidnappers strike anywhere on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao, snatching people from streets, offices and beach resorts.
But despite a wave of abductions, businessmen remain positive about the region's economy, torn by decades of war.

"It worries us, but once this thing is over, the good times will come," a local businessman said after Moslem guerrillas seized Japanese businessman Kenichi Takayama and three Filipinos from a beach in southern Mindanao this week.
Soldiers rescued the four captives on Tuesday, killing two kidnappers in a mountainside skirmish.
On Wednesday, kidnappers disguised as preachers struck in another town, abducting a businessman who had just stepped from his car in Iligan city.
Of about 100 people, mostly businessmen, known to have been kidnapped in the Philippines since January, half were nabbed on Mindanao, the ancestral homeland of the country's five million Moslems.
Some were seized from their cars. Others were in their homes or offices when they were grabbed by captors, sometimes dressed in police uniforms.
Dubbed "the land of promise", Mindanao's waters teem with fish, the land is rich in minerals, and agricultural produce helps feed the rest of this largely Christian country of 70 million.
MOSLEM AREAS REMAIN POOR
Despite the region's natural wealth, its Moslem-dominated areas have remained poor.

Analysts blame the poverty on official neglect, political corruption and a long history of violence between rival Moslem political factions and, since the 1970s, between Manila and guerrilla groups fighting for Moslem self-rule.
A peace deal with the government signed 10 months ago has placated the mainstream Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), but bloodshed continues to plague the land.
Two other insurgent groups still defy the government while kidnap gangs, led by renegade guerrillas, continue to bring terror to Christian communities, mainly in Cotabato city.
President Fidel Ramos averted a threat by Cotabato Christians to close their businesses in protest against the kidnapping scourge by sending elite troops to the city last month.
But the kidnappers simply moved elsewhere. On Sunday, they struck for the first time on nearby Sarangani island, snatching Takayama. Three days later, they appeared in priestly robes in Iligan.
Businessmen in General Santos, a Christian boomtown 80 km (50 miles) north of Sarangani, are worried the kidnapping menace might spill over into their backyard.

"If the government cannot put an end to this, it will certainly affect potential investors. Even those who are here may have second thoughts about their plans to expand," said Regino Miguel, vice-president of the General Santos Chamber of Commerce.
BUSINESS STILL HAS FAITH IN REGION

But Guillermo Luz, executive director of Manila's prestigious Makati Business Club, said although areas in Mindanao affected by lawlessness might have difficulty luring investment, business still had faith in the region's potential.
"They are quite bullish about the outlook for Iligan, Davao, Cagayan de Oro, General Santos," Luz said, naming some of Mindanao's main cities.

"Generally there has been a positive outlook, also because of linkages with the East ASEAN Growth Area" -- a scheme to develop the adjacent provinces of the southern Philippines, eastern Malaysia, northern Indonesia and Brunei.
The trade department predicted in a report in May that Mindanao's economy would take off, with an annual growth rate of seven percent from 1997 to 1999.

Since the peace accord with the MNLF, Manila has poured $1.6 billion into the region for infrastructure and other projects. The report said about $2.8 billion more in investment was needed over the next five years.

Robert Sears, executive director of the American Chamber of Commerce, said the kidnapping of Takayama "would cause potential investors to perk up their ears and listen a bit more closely and to monitor the situation".
But a separate peace deal being negotiated by Manila with the hardline Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) should help break the cycle of violence.

"Mindanao has fantastic economic potential. Peace and order and increased economic activity will help resolve any problems they have there ... Once you have peace, economic activity and jobs will follow suit," Sears said.
